extracted.intended_audience: stand-up comedians and joke-writers (especially beginners/punch-up writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guide to common joke formats and techniques for writing and improving stand-up material, emphasizing creating 'comedic conflict' rather than mechanically following formats. Includes definitions, examples, pitfalls, and step-by-step writing tips for each technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use joke formats to learn and punch-up (don't write into formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main purpose of these lessons is NOT to learn conventional joke-writing strategies. The main purpose is to introduce practical, relatable examples of comedic conflict so you will be comfortable with the idea of comedic conflict when it comes time to write your own material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Joke formats are useful for: 1) Learning the basics of stand-up comedy and 2) Punching up your material. Quick Tips: Don't explicitly use these joke formats. If you ask 'Should I use a Rule of Three joke here?' you're likely being mechanical and choppy. Understand how to create comedic conflict and use formats as training or for punch-ups, not as the primary method of writing material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic Conflict framework (Safety / Violation / Shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes create a 'safety' (the audience's normal interpretation) and a 'violation' (the punchline which breaks an assumption). The punchline 'shifts' the original interpretation and produces laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always identify which piece(s) of information are explicit vs implicit (Who, What, Where, When, Why, How). Use the audience's implicit assumptions as safety; design the punchline to change one assumption (a 'shift'). Keep the safety strong to allow the violation to land. Many examples (e.g., Steve Martin, Bill Engvall) illustrate who-shifts, where safety is the assumed context and violation reveals something different.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broken Assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every time you speak you give explicit (said) and implicit (assumed) information about Who, What, Where, When, Why, and How. The punchline breaks one of the audience's assumptions to create humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: identify explicit info, let audience form assumptions, then deliver a punchline that shifts one assumption (a 'who-shift', 'where-shift', etc.). 'When' is often left out or kept vague to reduce noise ('the other day'). Audience comprehension proceeds through construction, recognition, and resolution—do not overload them with info. Leave out unnecessary details to make the shift easier to find.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration uses incongruity by stretching a key word/idea (size, emotional reaction, etc.) to make a story or punchline more interesting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to write exaggeration: 1) Write a few sentences about an experience; 2) Find ideas that can be exaggerated; 3) Rewrite or add exaggeration; 4) Polish for flow. Pitfalls: over-exaggeration harms trustworthiness and 'tears' the joke (too much violation); under-exaggeration is boring (too much safety). Play to find the optimum level of exaggeration; test and adjust until the exaggeration is funny but believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misplaced Sincerity
rubrics_metrics.description: The comedian pretends to lack knowledge or awareness of what the audience knows; the humor comes from the audience seeing both the comedian's naive POV and their own POV simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Safety = how a normal person would interpret something; Violation = comedian's incorrect interpretation. Writing steps: 1) Start with pre-written material; 2) Find phrases that are easy to misunderstand or require specific knowledge; 3) Ask 'What if I misunderstood this?'; 4) Write a follow-up that assumes you 'missed the point'. Use this technique to punch-up material rather than to write the whole joke from scratch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: A contradiction mixes misplaced sincerity, irony, and POV humor: the comedian says something that contradicts their words, actions, or the audience's knowledge about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two important characteristics: speed (must be fast—1–2 lines) and believability (must feel natural). Three types: 1) Words contradict Words (e.g., sarcastic delivery), 2) Words contradict Actions (say one thing then do another), 3) Words contradict What Audience Already Knows (line contradicts known persona). Write: start with pre-written material, decide who will make contradiction, find factual statements to contradict, create the circumstance that causes the contradiction, deliver contradiction quickly, and rewrite for flow. Sell contradictions with confidence and unawareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of Three
rubrics_metrics.description: List two similar items that create a pattern (safety) and a third that breaks the pattern (violation). The comedic conflict comes from breaking the audience's assumption about the third item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic structure: item1 + item2 (pattern) → item3 (breaks pattern). Pitfalls: modern audiences often expect the third item to be different; if you don't hide it well they'll anticipate a break and the setup loses power. Make sure to hide the pattern and deliver a good payoff; consider variations that obscure the 'third will differ' predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pun / Double-Entendre
rubrics_metrics.description: A linguistic comedic conflict using double-meanings. Puns use alternative meanings of words to create safety and violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types: single-step puns (one link), two-step puns (require an extra structure), and 'punch-to-setup' jokes (punchline-first then write a fitting setup). Practice with exercises (fill-in-the-blank). Pitfalls: puns are easy and common—low-quality puns feel like 'street-jokes'; high-quality puns must add something beyond obvious wordplay. Be careful not to overuse puns in stand-up.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-Jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes about jokes: use references to characterize or mock popular joke formats. The humor relies on the audience recognizing the joke-style being referenced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-jokes create the expectation of a 'normal finish' and then break that by making fun of the joke form itself. Examples: 'An Englishman, a Scotsman, and an Irishman walk into a bar...' where punchline comments on the joke form. Meta-jokes can highlight absurdity of common joke types and were popularized by 'anti-comedians' like Steve Martin and Albert Brooks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Callback Lines
rubrics_metrics.description: A callback is a line that references something used earlier in the set; it 'calls back' to an earlier punchline or reference and repurposes it in a new context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Callbacks are powerful because they invoke the earlier joke's entire context with just a short phrase, creating an 'inside joke' and community with the audience. Key characteristics: the audience needs to forget the original line enough that the callback surprises them; timing (longer sets give more power); the callback must make sense in the new context; callbacks are especially effective as show endings. Use callbacks sparingly and place them later in the set for maximum effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omitted Punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Intentionally leave out the last word(s) of a punchline so the audience fills in the rest—often substituted with a gesture or pause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements: you MUST give the audience enough information to fill in the punchline the way you want. Most omitted punchlines use gesture or pause as the missing words. Benefits: increases playfulness, audience participation, and can make violations feel safer because the audience supplied the content. Technique: use vocal inflection, gestures, and timing to guide the audience to the intended completion; follow with a tag if useful. Pitfall: if clues are ambiguous, audience may fill with something unintended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speciﬁcity
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace vague nouns/ideas with specific choices to create clearer, funnier mental images and to add a 'second layer' of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specificity doesn't create the comedic conflict but enhances storytelling and punchlines. Brand names are useful because audiences share knowledge about them and brands carry connotations (e.g., 'Volvo' = safety) that add ironic layers. How to write specificity: identify general nouns, list specific alternatives, pick the one that adds the most comedic conflict or flavor, and replace it. Specificity aligns audience imagery and can add an extra ironic twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-Depreciation (bonus lesson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice prompts and techniques for self-deprecating humor (labeled 'Self-Depreciation' in the guide) — using your own flaws/misfortunes as material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided practice setup/punchline combinations and guidance on how to complete them: link the premise to a punchline that keeps enough safety while delivering the self-deprecating violation. Use questions like 'What would parents put in a bathtub if they hated their child?' and guidance on direction for each prompt. Use self-deprecation to create relatable humility while avoiding mean-spiritedness.
